conversations.title: Parkinson’s drastically changed how they have sex. They're not alone.
conversations.reply: A neurologist naming this out loud is rare, and testimony from disabled daters explains why: people flinch at anything unscripted about disability and sex, then go quiet rather than ask one honest question. That silence gets treated as normal far more than the condition itself.

conversations.title: The founder of Hinge raised $18M to build a new AI dating service, Overtone
conversations.reply: Another $18m for an app built by the same industry that has spent years failing to ask disabled daters a single honest question. Testimony from disabled daters is consistent across every mainstream platform, AI polish included: the vanishing act after disclosure never went away.

conversations.title: Column | Asking Eric: Neighbors react badly to person with autism disorder
conversations.reply: A neighbour treating autism as grounds for open hostility is not a personality clash, it is ableism with a garden fence. Testimony from disabled people living this says the same thing on repeat: the discrimination rarely announces itself, it just turns up as rudeness nobody has to justify.

conversations.title: Leeds Pride 2026 Set to Draw 60,000 as City Marks 20 Years of Celebration
conversations.reply: 60,000 in the city centre is the headline; whether the step-free routes and venues actually exist for wheelchair users on the night is the test that press release never answers. Testimony from disabled Pride-goers says the same thing every year: access gets promised, then quietly drops off before the parade starts.

conversations.title: Co-op extends festival sponsorship deal with Live Nation until 2031
conversations.reply: Five more years of convenience stores at UK festivals, while testimony from disabled festivalgoers keeps asking what this deal never answers: what about the gate, the campsite, the sightline to the stage. Sponsorship deals get renewed for years; accessible festival infrastructure barely gets a mention in the same breath.

conversations.title: Elle King Shares How Autism Diagnosis Changed Her Life
conversations.reply: A diagnosis reshaping how someone sees their life is testimony heard constantly in the disability community. The part that rarely makes headlines is what happens next in dating: the disclosure moment, and the people who quietly disappear right after it.

target_reply: Testimony from blind daters says the same thing on repeat: platforms build without accessibility in mind, then act surprised when disabled users leave without a word said out loud. Able2Love exists precisely because that pattern was never challenged by the mainstream apps.
funding: Nothing new today. Ongoing routes worth knowing: UnLtd (unltd.org.uk), Access to Work (gov.uk), Stelios Awards (around March).
moment: July is Disability Pride Month. The honest way to mark it: check whether the venue for tonight's plans actually has step-free access before you post about inclusion, not after.

instagram_hitlist.who: Disabled dating or interabled relationship creators who post about disclosure conversations and how matches react once they know
instagram_hitlist.why: This is exactly the pattern the testimony describes: warm messages before disclosure, silence after it, dressed up as 'it's not you, it's me'
instagram_hitlist.comment: That disappearing act after disclosure is not a one-off, it is the most consistent story disabled daters tell, and it rarely gets named this plainly.

instagram_hitlist.who: #disabilitydating, browsing for posts where people vent about mainstream apps ghosting them after finding out about a visible disability
instagram_hitlist.why: Directly matches the core position: daters are not upfront, they vanish, and the excuse is never the honest one
instagram_hitlist.comment: Read the comments under posts like this and the same story repeats itself endlessly: all the right words, then gone the moment a visible disability is disclosed.

instagram_hitlist.who: Manchester-based accessibility or access-fail accounts that photograph steps, no ramps or missing step-free entrances at venues and events
instagram_hitlist.why: Feeds the nightlife exclusion theme directly, with a named local pattern rather than an abstract complaint
instagram_hitlist.comment: A venue with a step at the door has already decided who the night is for, whatever the flyer says about being open to everyone.

instagram_hitlist.who: #wheelchairlife, looking for a recent access win, a venue or event that actually got step-free entry right
instagram_hitlist.why: Matches the instruction to celebrate access wins properly with warmth rather than snark
instagram_hitlist.comment: More of this, please. Getting through a door on the first attempt should not be the exception worth posting about, but until it stops being one, keep flagging it.

instagram_hitlist.who: Accounts covering Manchester's Gay Village, Pride or club nights from a disabled clubber's perspective, especially ones calling out 'inclusive' events with no step-free access
instagram_hitlist.why: Central to the core position on nightlife exclusion and false inclusivity claims
instagram_hitlist.comment: An 'inclusive' night that wheelchair users cannot physically get into is not inclusive, it is a party with an unwritten door policy, and whole scenes still get away with running exactly like this.

instagram_hitlist.who: #invisibledisability, searching for testimony about being believed less, or partners disappearing once a hidden condition is disclosed
instagram_hitlist.why: Extends the disclosure-then-vanish pattern beyond visible disability, reinforcing the same tested position with different testimony
instagram_hitlist.comment: Same pattern, different disability: honest disclosure met with silence, then some vague line about timing or compatibility that everyone recognises for what it actually is.
